leads.text: HTTP request smuggling (CWE-444) in Message.set_body_reader: the header loop accepts Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length simultaneously without rejecting the conflict, and silently IGNORES every Transfer-Encoding value that is not exactly "chunked". Line 134-136 is `elif name == "TRANSFER-ENCODING": if value.lower() == "chunked": chunked = True` with NO else-branch that raises. Then line 139 `if chunked:` -> ChunkedReader, line 140 `elif content_length is not None:` -> LengthReader. Two concrete desyncs: (a) CL.TE -- a request with both `Content-Length: 6` and `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` is accepted; gunicorn frames the body with ChunkedReader while a front-end proxy honoring Content-Length frames it differently, so trailing bytes become a smuggled pipelined request; (b) TE obfuscation -- `Transfer-Encoding: chunked, identity` / `xchunked` / `chunked ` fails the exact `== "chunked"` test, so gunicorn ignores TE entirely and falls back to Content-Length, while a proxy that substring-matches or last-token-matches "chunked" uses chunked framing. Request.set_body_reader (line 357) overrides this but adds ONLY an EOFReader->LengthReader(0) substitution (line 359-360), so it introduces no TE/CL conflict validation.

leads.text: HTTP request smuggling (CWE-444) via non-RFC chunk sizes in ChunkedReader.parse_chunk_size: line 88 computes `chunk_size = line.split(b";",1)[0].strip()` and line 90 parses it with `int(chunk_size, 16)`, whose only guard is `except ValueError` (line 92). Python's int(x,16) accepts forms that RFC 7230 chunk-size forbids: a leading sign (`int(b"-1",16) == -1`), an explicit `0x` prefix (`int(b"0x10",16) == 16`), and PEP-515 underscores (`int(b"1_0",16) == 16`). There is NO `chunk_size < 0` check -- line 94 only tests `if chunk_size == 0:` (which is the branch that consumes trailers and returns (0,None)), so a negative size falls through to line 100 `return (chunk_size, rest_chunk)`. In parse_chunked the loop head is line 59 `while size > 0:`, so a negative size exits the loop immediately and the body generator terminates WITHOUT ever validating a terminating 0-length chunk; the unconsumed socket bytes stay buffered in the unreader and are parsed as the next pipelined request on the keep-alive connection. Attack: send `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` with a first chunk-size line of `-1` (or `0x10`/`1_0`), followed by a smuggled request -- any front-end proxy that rejects or differently interprets these forms desynchronizes from gunicorn.

leads.text: Client-controlled SCRIPT_NAME request header is trusted into the WSGI environ, and also yields an unhandled IndexError remote DoS. In wsgi.create() the loop over req.headers at line 127-128 does `elif hdr_name == "SCRIPT_NAME": script_name = hdr_value` -- hdr_name is the request header name uppercased by message.py:92 (`name = name.upper()`), so any client sending a header literally named `Script_Name:` / `SCRIPT_NAME:` sets it. HEADER_RE (message.py:24) is a blocklist `[\x00-\x1F\x7F()<>@,;:\[\]={} \t\\\"]` that does NOT contain underscore, so the underscore name passes header-name validation. The value then reaches `environ['SCRIPT_NAME'] = script_name` (line 185), controlling the WSGI app's mount-point/routing and URL generation. Critically, line 183 computes `path_info = path_info.split(script_name, 1)[1]`: if script_name is not a substring of req.path, split returns a 1-element list and the `[1]` index raises IndexError, an unhandled exception in request setup -- e.g. `GET / HTTP/1.1` with `Script_Name: /nomatch` gives `"/".split("/nomatch",1)` == `["/"]` -> IndexError. I verified there is NO trust gating on this path: a query for any forwarded_allow_ips / peer_addr / secure_scheme reference anywhere in gunicorn/http/wsgi.py returned 0 rows, so unlike the scheme headers (gated in message.py:70-75) and PROXY protocol (gated by proxy_allow_ips in message.py:280-283), SCRIPT_NAME is accepted from any peer.

leads.text: Proxy-header spoofing via underscore/dash collision when building the WSGI environ (CWE-444 inconsistent interpretation). wsgi.create() line 136 computes `key = 'HTTP_' + hdr_name.replace('-', '_')`, and lines 137-139 MERGE a repeated key by concatenation: `if key in environ: hdr_value = "%s,%s" % (environ[key], hdr_value)` then `environ[key] = hdr_value`. Because HEADER_RE (message.py:24) does not blocklist underscore, a request header named `X_Forwarded_For` is a valid header name and maps to the SAME environ key `HTTP_X_FORWARDED_FOR` as the dashed `X-Forwarded-For`. A front-end proxy that strips/overwrites only the dashed spelling will not touch the underscored one, so the attacker's value is comma-merged into the trusted header the application reads for client-IP/ACL decisions -- letting the attacker prepend or append arbitrary entries to X-Forwarded-For (and equivalently to any other HTTP_* header the app trusts). No deduplication or underscore rejection exists on this path.

leads.text: Request method is effectively unvalidated past its first few characters, flowing to environ['REQUEST_METHOD'] and the access log (CWE-20). message.py:25 defines `METH_RE = re.compile(r"[A-Z0-9$-_.]{3,20}")` and line 336 tests it with `if not METH_RE.match(bits[0])`. Two compounding defects: (1) the pattern has NO end anchor (`$`/`\Z`) and `re.match` anchors only at the start, so once the first 3 characters match the class the ENTIRE remainder of the token is unchecked and arbitrary -- `bits[0]` is only bounded by the whitespace split at line 331 (`line_bytes.split(None, 2)`); (2) the character class contains `$-_`, which Python parses as a RANGE from \x24 to \x5F, silently admitting `%&'()*+,-./0123456789:;<=>?@`, `[`, `\`, `]` and `^` rather than the intended literal `$`, `-`, `_`. The value is then stored at line 338 (`self.method = bits[0].upper()`) and propagated to `environ["REQUEST_METHOD"] = req.method` (wsgi.py:83/86) and into the access-log atoms 'm' and 'r' (glogging.py:297-303), so a downstream app, proxy or log consumer that treats the method differently from gunicorn can be desynchronized or injected into.

leads.text: Response status line is written without the CRLF/control-character validation that gunicorn applies to every other response header (CWE-113 response splitting). Response.start_response stores the app-supplied status verbatim at wsgi.py:233 (`self.status = status`); the only subsequent operation is line 239 `self.status_code = int(self.status.split()[0])`, whose failure is swallowed into `self.status_code = None` at line 241. default_headers then interpolates it straight into the status line at line 304-306: `"HTTP/%s.%s %s\r\n" % (self.req.version[0], self.req.version[1], self.status)`, and send_headers (line 318-319) emits it. By contrast process_headers validates header NAMES with HEADER_RE (line 252-253) and header VALUES with `HEADER_VALUE_RE = re.compile(r'[\x00-\x1F\x7F]')` (wsgi.py:21, checked at line 258-259) -- status bypasses both. A WSGI application that places request-derived text into its status reason-phrase (a pattern that is safe on servers which validate status) therefore permits header/body injection into the response. This is second-order: it needs the hosted app to pass attacker-influenced status, so it is a missing-defense gap rather than a directly reachable flow -- ranked lowest for that reason.

leads.text: METH_RE = re.compile(r"[A-Z0-9$-_.]{3,20}") in gunicorn/http/message.py:25 has TWO compounding defects in the literal/usage pair, and it is the only validation applied to the attacker-supplied HTTP request method. (1) `$-_` inside the character class is parsed by Python's re as a RANGE 0x24-0x5F, not three literal chars, so the class silently admits `% & ' ( ) * + , - . / 0-9 : ; < = > ? @ A-Z [ \ ] ^ _` -- e.g. a method of `@@@` or `///` or `<<<` passes. (2) It is applied with `.match()` (line 336), which anchors only at the START and has no trailing `$`/`fullmatch`, so the `{3,20}` upper bound is never enforced and arbitrary trailing bytes are accepted: `METH_RE.match("GET" + <anything>)` succeeds on the 3-char prefix. Because bits[0] comes from `bytes_to_str` = `str(b,'latin1')` (gunicorn/util.py:650), every raw byte 0x00-0xFF reaches this check 1:1. The accepted token is then stored verbatim as `self.method = bits[0].upper()` (line 338) and forwarded as REQUEST_METHOD, so a reverse proxy and gunicorn can disagree on where the method token ends -> request smuggling / method confusion. parse_request_line is an :EntryPoint handler (hop_distance 0).

leads.text: The `strip_header_spaces` config flag is an in-repo switch that DISABLES the HEADER_RE whitespace guard in the request header parser, and gunicorn's own setting description calls it out as a known vulnerability. In gunicorn/http/message.py:24, HEADER_RE = re.compile(r"[\x00-\x1F\x7F()<>@,;:\[\]={} \t\\\"]") — the rejected character class INCLUDES space and tab, so a header name like "Content-Length " (trailing space before the colon) is normally rejected at line 93-94 (`if HEADER_RE.search(name): raise InvalidHeaderName(name)`). But at line 89 `if self.cfg.strip_header_spaces:` line 90 runs `name = name.rstrip(" \t").upper()`, stripping the space/tab BEFORE the line-93 check can see it; the safe else-branch at line 92 is just `name = name.upper()`, which preserves the space so HEADER_RE fires. With the flag on, `Content-Length :` / `Transfer-Encoding :` are silently normalized to valid CONTENT-LENGTH / TRANSFER-ENCODING headers and accepted as authoritative framing headers. Config setting at gunicorn/config.py:2244-2251 whose desc reads: "Strip spaces present between the header name and the the ``:``. This is known to induce vulnerabilities and is not compliant with the HTTP/1.1 standard. See https://portswigger.net/research/http-desync-attacks-request-smuggling-reborn. Use with care and only if necessary." A front-end proxy that does NOT treat `Content-Length :` as Content-Length while gunicorn does yields a front-end/back-end framing disagreement = HTTP request smuggling / desync. The flag site is reachable_from_entry=true at hop_distance=1 and the enclosing method Message.parse_headers is hop_distance=0.

leads.text: The `ssl_version` security control has been REVERTED TO A NO-OP: its validator now only prints a deprecation warning and the value is never consumed when the SSLContext is built, so an operator who pins a minimum TLS version to forbid legacy protocols gets that control silently discarded. gunicorn/config.py:366-368 defines `validate_ssl_version` whose entire body is `if val != SSLVersion.default: sys.stderr.write("Warning: option `ssl_version` is deprecated and it is ignored. Use ssl_context instead.\n")` — it warns and falls through, returning no enforced value. The SSLVersion setting (config.py:2099-2110) wires `validator = validate_ssl_version` and its own desc states ".. deprecated:: 20.2  The option is deprecated and it is currently ignored." A query for every CpgCall mentioning `ssl_version` across the whole scan returns ZERO hits in gunicorn/sock.py, the module that actually constructs the server SSLContext — sock.py only reads conf.cert_reqs (line 220), conf.suppress_ragged_eofs and conf.do_handshake_on_connect (lines 229-231). So `--ssl-version=TLSv1_2` is accepted on the CLI, warns to stderr, and then has no effect on the negotiated protocol floor.

leads.text: The forwarded_allow_ips front-end IP allowlist — the protection that stops clients from forging the secure-scheme headers — can be fully disabled, and is ALREADY bypassed unconditionally for non-tuple peer addresses regardless of configuration. At gunicorn/http/message.py:72-75 the guard is `if '*' in cfg.forwarded_allow_ips or not isinstance(self.peer_addr, tuple) or self.peer_addr[0] in cfg.forwarded_allow_ips: secure_scheme_headers = cfg.secure_scheme_headers`. The middle disjunct `not isinstance(self.peer_addr, tuple)` means that whenever peer_addr is not a tuple (e.g. a Unix-domain-socket listener), the IP allowlist is skipped entirely even if the operator configured a strict one. Once secure_scheme_headers is populated, lines 111-119 let the request's own headers flip the connection scheme: `if name in secure_scheme_headers: secure = value == secure_scheme_headers[name]; scheme = "https" if secure else "http" ... self.scheme = scheme`. The defaults (config.py:1227-1230) trust X-FORWARDED-PROTOCOL=ssl, X-FORWARDED-PROTO=https, X-FORWARDED-SSL=on, so a client that reaches gunicorn directly can assert its plaintext connection is HTTPS, defeating downstream SSL-redirect/secure-cookie logic. config.py:1265 documents the kill switch: "Set to ``*`` to disable checking of Front-end IPs", and the default is environment-overridable via `os.environ.get("FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS", "127.0.0.1")` (config.py:1264) — a container image or orchestrator setting FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS=* disables the check with no code change. parse_headers is reachable_from_entry=true at hop_distance=0.

leads.text: VERSION_RE = re.compile(r"HTTP/(\d+)\.(\d+)") in gunicorn/http/message.py:26 is unanchored at BOTH ends and is applied with `.match()` at line 352 to the attacker-controlled HTTP-version token, so trailing garbage is silently accepted and discarded. Critically, the request line is tokenized as `line_bytes.split(None, 2)` (line 331) with maxsplit=2, so bits[2] is the entire remainder of the line and MAY CONTAIN SPACES. A request line `GET / HTTP/1.1 <arbitrary text>` yields bits[2]="HTTP/1.1 <arbitrary text>", `VERSION_RE.match` matches the "HTTP/1.1" prefix, `match is None` is False (line 353), and `self.version = (int(match.group(1)), int(match.group(2)))` = (1,1) -- the trailing text is dropped with no error. There is no `$` / `fullmatch` and no length bound on `\d+`, so `HTTP/0000000001.1` is also accepted. A front-end proxy that rejects or re-interprets that trailing text while gunicorn accepts it produces request-line desync / smuggling. parse_request_line is an :EntryPoint handler (hop_distance 0).

leads.text: HEADER_RE = re.compile(r"[\x00-\x1F\x7F()<>@,;:\[\]={} \t\\\"]") at gunicorn/http/message.py:24 is a DENYLIST (used as `if HEADER_RE.search(name): raise InvalidHeaderName(name)` at line 93) rather than an RFC-7230 token allowlist, and its character set stops at \x7F. Request bytes reach this check through `bytes_to_str` = `str(b,'latin1')` (gunicorn/util.py:650), which maps raw bytes 0x80-0xFF 1:1 onto codepoints U+0080-U+00FF -- none of which appear in the denylist. A request header name containing any high-bit byte (e.g. `X-Foo\xA0Bar: v`, or a name made entirely of 0x80-0xFF bytes) therefore passes validation and is admitted into self.headers, while RFC 7230 forbids those octets in a field-name. The literal also omits `/`, `?` and `'`, which are likewise non-token characters. Divergent header-name acceptance between gunicorn and a front-end proxy is the precondition for header/request smuggling. parse_headers is an :EntryPoint handler (hop_distance 0). The same HEADER_RE denylist is reused on the response path at gunicorn/http/wsgi.py:252 (Response.process_headers, centrality 7.2e-5 -- a chokepoint every response flows through).

leads.text: ReDoS-shaped regex literal: gunicorn/instrument/statsd.py:28 runs `sub(r"^(.+[^.]+)\.*$", "\\g<1>.", cfg.statsd_prefix)` in Statsd.__init__. The pattern places two adjacent unbounded quantifiers over overlapping character classes -- `.+` followed by `[^.]+`, where every character matched by `[^.]` is also matched by `.` -- and then requires `\.*$` to consume the remainder. On a non-matching subject the engine must enumerate every split point between `.+` and `[^.]+`, giving polynomial (quadratic) backtracking in the length of the input rather than the intended linear scan. The mitigating factor is the taint source: the subject is `cfg.statsd_prefix`, an operator-supplied config/CLI value, not request data, so this is a hardening/robustness item rather than a remotely reachable DoS -- it becomes exploitable only if an untrusted party controls statsd_prefix. Reported because it is the only nested/adjacent-quantifier regex literal in the first-party tree; a repo-wide scan for classic `(a+)+` / `(x*)*` catastrophic shapes returned zero first-party hits.

leads.text: Dynamic regex construction against an attacker-controlled subject: examples/multidomainapp.py:19 builds a pattern at match time with `re.match("^" + pattern + "$", host)`, where `host` is taken straight from the Host request header (`host = environ.get("HTTP_HOST", "")` at line 15, narrowed by `host.split(":")[0]` at line 16) and `pattern` is an un-validated, un-escaped string unpacked from the operator-supplied `self.mapping` (line 18). Two literal-level issues: (a) because the mapping entries are interpolated raw into a regex rather than passed through re.escape, any mapping entry containing a nested quantifier turns the Host header into a ReDoS trigger, and the regex is recompiled per request inside the request loop; (b) the shipped mapping literal at line 33 is `[("localhost", hello), (".*", bye)]`, whose `".*"` entry is an unconditional catch-all that matches ANY Host value, so the host-based routing it demonstrates provides no isolation at all. The shipped literals are not themselves catastrophic-backtracking shapes, and this is sample code under examples/ rather than the shipped gunicorn package, so impact is limited to copy-paste propagation into user apps.
